'''Henry Perigal, Jr.''' [[Royal Astronomical Society|FRAS]] [[Royal Institution|MRI]] (1 April 1801 – 6 June 1898) was a British stockbroker and [[amateur]] mathematician, known for his [[dissection problem|dissection]]-based proof of the [[Pythagorean theorem]] and for his unorthodox belief that the moon does not rotate.<ref name="dpf">{{citation|title=Dissections: Plane & Fancy|first=Greg N.|last=Frederickson|page=31|publisher=Cambridge University Press|year=1997}}.</ref><ref name="lms">{{citation|title=Tucker–Oakes Photograph |journal=LMS Newsletter |volume=391 |url=http://old.lms.ac.uk/newsletter/391/391_12.html |year=2010 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120403065046/http://old.lms.ac.uk/newsletter/391/391_12.html |archive-date=2012-04-03 }}.</ref><ref name="rms">{{citation|title=Proceedings at the meeting of the society. May 18, 1898. Ordinary Meeting|journal=Quarterly Journal of the Royal Meteorological Society|volume=24|issue=108|page=261|year=1898|doi=10.1002/qj.49702410806|bibcode = 1898QJRMS..24..261B |last1=Bayard|first1=Francis Campbell}}.</ref><ref name="gnf2">{{citation|title=A visit to the monument of Henry Perigal|first=Greg N.|last=Frederickson|year=1999|url=http://www.cs.purdue.edu/homes/gnf/book/Booknews/perig_m.html}}.</ref><ref name="casselman">{{citation|title=On the dissecting table: Henry Perigal 1801 - 1898|journal=Plus Magazine|volume=16|date=December 2000|url=http://plus.maths.org/content/dissecting-table}}.</ref><ref name="mnras">{{citation|title=Obituary Notices : Fellows :- Perigal, Henry|journal=[[Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society]]|volume=59|issue=5|pages=226–228|year=1899|bibcode=1899MNRAS..59R.226.|doi=10.1093/mnras/59.5.226a|doi-access=free}}</ref>

==Biography==
Perigal descended from a [[Huguenot]] family who emigrated to England in the late 17th century,<ref name="gnf2"/><ref name="casselman"/><ref name="mnras"/> and was the oldest of six siblings.<ref name="mnras"/> After working as a clerk for the [[Privy Council of the United Kingdom|Privy Council]], he became a bookkeeper in a London stockbrokerage in the 1840s.<ref name="casselman"/><ref name="mnras"/> He remained a lifelong bachelor.<ref name="dpf"/>

Perigal was a member of the [[London Mathematical Society]] from 1868 to 1897,<ref name="lms"/> and was treasurer of the [[Royal Meteorological Society]] for 45 years, from 1853 until his death in 1898.<ref name="rms"/> He was elected as a [[fellow]] of the [[Royal Astronomical Society]] in 1850.<ref name="mnras"/> He attended the [[Royal Institution]] regularly as a visitor for many years, and finally became a member in 1895, at age 94.<ref name="dpf"/><ref name="mnras"/> Friends with [[Washington Teasdale]] and [[James Glaisher]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Washington Teasdale |url=https://www.mhs.ox.ac.uk/collections/imu-search-page/narratives/?irn=14221&index=1 |website=History of Science Museum, Oxford |access-date=18 August 2019}}</ref>
He was an original member of the British Astronomical Association in 1890; he would be oldest member of the BAA if all the members were gathered together.  
Although Perigal was long-lived, his father lived even longer, becoming a [[centenarian]].<ref name="casselman"/>

==Mathematics==
[[File:Perigal 1891 p1.jpg|thumb|Page 1 of ''Geometric Dissections and Transpositions'', showing Perigal's dissection-based proof of the Pythagorean theorem]]
In his booklet [[s:Geometric Dissections and Transpositions|''Geometric Dissections and Transpositions'']] (London: Bell & Sons, 1891) Perigal provided a proof of the [[Pythagorean theorem]] based on the idea of [[dissection problem|dissecting]] two smaller squares into a larger square. The five-piece dissection that he found may be generated by overlaying a regular square tiling whose [[prototile]] is the larger square with a [[Pythagorean tiling]] generated by the two smaller squares.<ref name="dpf"/><ref name="rbn">{{citation|title=Paintings, plane tilings, and proofs|first=Roger B.|last=Nelsen|journal=[[Math Horizons]]|date=November 2003|volume=11|issue=2|pages=5–8|doi=10.1080/10724117.2003.12021741|s2cid=126000048|url=http://www-stat.wharton.upenn.edu/~steele/Publications/Books/CSMC/New%20Problems/paintings.pdf}}. Reprinted in {{citation|title=The Edge of the Universe: Celebrating Ten Years of Math Horizons|series=Spectrum Series|publisher=Mathematical Association of America|first1=Deanna|last1=Haunsperger|first2=Stephen|last2=Kennedy|year=2007|isbn=978-0-88385-555-3|pages=295–298}}.</ref> Perigal had the same dissection printed on his business cards, and it also appears on his tombstone,<ref name="dpf"/><ref name="casselman"/> which is located within the grounds of [[St Mary and St Peter's Church, Wennington|St Mary and St Peter]], [[Wennington, London|Wennington]], [[Essex]], now the [[London Borough of Havering]].<ref>Pevsner, Cherry, Bradley. "London: East", p. 216.</ref>

In the same book, Perigal expressed the hope that dissection based methods would also solve the 1925 Tarski's problem of [[Tarski's circle-squaring problem|circle-squaring by dissection]]. That problem had been shown to be impossible to solve in a constructive way in 1963.<ref>{{citation|title=Scissor congruence|first1=Lester|last1=L. Dubins|first2=Morris|last2=Hirsch|first3=Jack|last3=Karush|date=1963|journal=[[Israel Journal of Mathematics]]|volume=1|issue=4|pages=239–247|doi=10.1007/BF02759727|doi-access=|s2cid=189795492}}</ref> Nevertheless, a non-constructive solution has been proposed by [[Miklós Laczkovich]] in 1990.<ref>{{citation|title=The Circle-Squaring Problem Decomposed|first1=Pamela|last1=Pierce|first2=John|last2=Ramsay|first3=Hannah|last3=Roberts|first4=Nancy|last4=Tinoza|first5=Jeffrey|last5=Willert|first6=Wenyuan|last6=Wu|journal=[[Math Horizons]]|url=https://www.maa.org/sites/default/files/pdf/upload_library/22/Evans/Pierce.pdf|date=November 2009|volume=17|issue=2|pages=19–21, 33|doi=10.1080/10724117.2009.11974849|s2cid=121884243}}.</ref>

Perigal also proposed the first 6-pieces solution to the [[square trisection]] problem.

As well as being interested in mathematics, Perigal was an accomplished [[lathe]] worker, and made models of mathematical curves for [[Augustus De Morgan]]. He falsely believed that the moon does not rotate with respect to the fixed stars, and used his knowledge of curvilinear motion in an attempt to demonstrate this belief to others.<ref name="dpf"/><ref name="casselman"/>
